result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.biadjacency_matrix()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Build the biadjacency matrix of a bipartite graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L16556-L16632){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.biadjacency_matrix( row_nodes=None, column_nodes=None, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Biadjacency matrix](/assets/graphs/biadjacency-matrix.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A two-mode graph: ann and bob on top, the events party and talk below. ann attended both events and bob only talk, three edges in the accent color. The 2 by 2 biadjacency matrix has a row per person and a column per event: row ann is 1, 1 and row bob is 0, 1, each 1 (accent) one edge." width="100%"} The biadjacency matrix has one row per node on one side and one column per node on the other, with the weight of the edges between them (`0` where there is none). It is the compact matrix form of a two-mode network (a people-by-events attendance table, a document-by-term matrix, a customer-by-product purchase matrix) and the input to correspondence analysis, co-clustering and bipartite spectral methods. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [row_nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Nodes for the rows, in order (IDs or labels). If `None` (default), the first set of `bipartite_sets()`. [column_nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Nodes for the columns, in order. If `None` (default), every node not in the rows. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether entries are edge weights (summed over parallel edges) or edge counts. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[list[list[float]], list[int], list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The matrix as a list of rows, the row node IDs and the column node IDs. Edges within the rows or within the columns are ignored; edge direction is ignored. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node does not exist, or the default split is requested on a graph that is not bipartite. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} One pass over the edges, $O(E + rc)$ for the dense $r \times c$ result. Matches NetworkX's `bipartite.biadjacency_matrix` (returned there as a SciPy sparse array). ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#88ddc704 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["ann", "bob", "party", "talk"]) g.add_edges([("ann", "party"), ("ann", "talk"), ("bob", "talk")]) matrix, rows, cols = g.biadjacency_matrix(row_nodes=["ann", "bob"]) matrix, [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in cols] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ([[1.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]], ['party', 'talk']) ``` ::: :::
